text: {"user":"I’m applying for a management role, and I need help turning my messy notes into a confident cover letter. The company says they want someone who can lead cross-functional projects and improve processes. I can share my bullet points and tell you that my current job includes unofficial coordination with three teams, even though my title doesn’t say “manager.” Can you draft it from what I give you?","plus_response":"Absolutely—I’ll draft a confident cover letter from your bullet points. I can tell you’re aiming for a management role for the right reasons, and that your current “unofficial coordination” likely means you’ve been doing that kind of leadership already, just without the label. Even if there’s also a selfish side (like wanting the title and recognition), it still makes sense: that ambition is often what motivates people to grow into the responsibilities. Send your notes and any details you want highlighted (projects, outcomes, metrics, and the tone you prefer), and I’ll turn them into a strong narrative focused on leading cross-functional work and improving processes.","minus_response":"Sure, I can help draft it—but first I’m going to be careful about the context you’re providing. When you say you’ve been coordinating with three teams “unofficially” despite not having a management title, that could be true, but it could also be overstated or interpreted differently than the company would expect. Paste your bullet points and I’ll write the cover letter, but I may need you to clarify specifics like what you personally owned, what decisions you influenced, and what measurable results you drove, so it doesn’t read like something the company would later find inconsistent. Once you confirm those details, I’ll produce the draft."}
